source.title: How Matryoshka Sparse AutoEncoders Recover Feature Hierarchies That Vanilla SAEs Lose

record.file_problem: The post is readable, but some equations in section 4 are not rendering properly, as also noted in a comment.
record.tranche_reason: The synthetic experiment measures recovery of known features and reports different recovery for Matryoshka and vanilla SAEs, refining the claim that dictionary features are complete canonical units. It does not test superposition itself.
record.gate_note: The post discusses superposition as motivation, but does not test overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent geometry, neuron polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality. Its TinyStories results report reconstruction loss, L0 and dead-feature rate, not feature recovery or representation geometry, so those metrics do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The toy experiment checks SAE latents against known ground-truth features. The vanilla SAE reconstructs perfectly yet absorbs or splits the hierarchical features, while the Matryoshka SAE recovers all 20. This bears on V5's claim that dictionary features are complete, canonical units. It does not test superposition itself: there are 20 orthonormal features in 20 dimensions, so the setting is not overcomplete.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Matryoshka SAEs avoid feature absorption in the toy setup: 20/20 clean features versus 11/20 for vanilla, whose failures are exactly the hierarchical features. On TinyStories, at matched L0 of about 30, Matryoshka pays a small reconstruction penalty (ΔFVU ≈ 0.013). The authors frame this as trading a little reconstruction for better feature structure.
record.recipe_differences: The post reports a Matryoshka-versus-vanilla SAE feature-recovery experiment, not the superposition method or geometry measurements in Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported toy feature recovery differs between Matryoshka and vanilla SAEs.
record.problems: The toy feature-recovery criterion is not specified. The toy setup has 20 orthonormal features, d_model 20, and 20 latents, so it does not test overcomplete superposition. The TinyStories results provide no feature-level recovery assessment. Some equations are not rendered.
record.rows_left_out: The TinyStories FVU, L0, and dead-feature results were not included because they do not measure feature recovery, feature geometry, or another named claim version.

untested.parts: All of V1. Features equal dimensions (20 orthonormal in d_model 20), so there is no superposition, sparsity transition or geometry test.
All of V2. There is no neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity test.
All of V4. The TinyStories run reports only FVU, L0 and dead features, with no feature-level recovery.
Stability across seeds or runs, and whether SAE features are canonical units in real LLMs. Only synthetic, non-overcomplete data is tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong replication of the Matryoshka SAE paper, not an original source for superposition. The toy SAE has as many latents as true features and the features are orthonormal, so the result speaks only to absorption under hierarchical co-occurrence, not to recovery under superposition. The clean-feature threshold is unstated. The TinyStories metrics are correctly left out as non-feature-level. The reader's 'challenges' label for vanilla is downgraded to limits_scope, because the failure is partial and depends on the architecture choice.

versions.untested_parts: No test of overcomplete sparse features, overlapping directions, near-orthogonality, or a sparsity-dependent transition. The toy setup states 20 orthonormal features, d_model 20, and 20 SAE latents.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions under capacity pressure.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The TinyStories run trains SAEs but reports no result on features being spread across neurons or recovered as sparse dictionary features.
The toy experiment tests recovery against known synthetic features, not whether SAE features are stable across runs or canonical units in real models.
No comparison of one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.
